pi.name: Sarah E. Kargbo-Hill
pi.title: Assistant Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Sarah E. Kargbo-Hill earned a B.S. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from Penn State University (2012), where she worked with Melissa Rolls on microtubule polarity in Drosophila neurons, and a Ph.D. in Cell Biology from Yale University (2018) with Daniel Colon-Ramos studying presynaptic development and autophagy in C. elegans. She completed postdoctoral training with Michael Ward at the NIH, using human iPSC-derived neurons to study neurodegenerative disease proteins such as TDP-43. She joined the MCDB department at the University of Michigan as an Assistant Professor in January 2024. Her training was supported by an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, a BrightFocus Foundation Fellowship, and a K99 NIH/NIA Pathway to Independence Award.

lab_description: The Kargbo-Hill Lab studies how neurons, as non-dividing cells that must survive for a lifetime, regulate gene expression to adapt to changing and sometimes stressful conditions. The lab focuses on two mechanisms, RNA splicing and active DNA demethylation, and how they are specialized in neurons and altered during aging and neurodegeneration. A central theme is the RNA-binding protein TDP-43, whose nuclear loss drives cryptic exon inclusion in ALS, frontotemporal dementia, and Alzheimer's disease. The lab combines human iPSC-derived neurons, the nematode C. elegans, live imaging, and multi-omics (epigenomic, transcriptomic, splicing, and proteomic) approaches.

research_areas.title: TDP-43 and RNA splicing in neurodegeneration
research_areas.summary: Investigates how TDP-43 regulates splicing and how its translocation from nucleus to cytosol in ALS, FTD, and Alzheimer's disease leads to cryptic exon inclusion that reduces target gene expression. Work in human iPSC-derived neurons identified novel pathologic splicing in the ALS/TDP-associated synaptic gene UNC13A.

research_areas.title: RNA splicing in C. elegans
research_areas.summary: Uses the nematode's ubiquitously expressed TDP-43 ortholog, TDP-1, to explore tissue-specific mechanisms of cryptic splicing regulation, taking advantage of the worm's optical accessibility and conserved RNA metabolism for studies of neuronal aging.

research_areas.title: Neuronal DNA (de)methylation
research_areas.summary: Examines active DNA demethylation as a gene regulatory mechanism in non-dividing neurons, building on the discovery that neurons undergo widespread DNA synthesis at enhancers to repair recurrent single-stranded DNA breaks, and asks how this is used during acute stress responses.

joining: The lab is actively recruiting at multiple levels. Postdoctoral applicants should send a CV with publication list and a cover letter explaining their research interests. Graduate students from the MCDB, PIBS, and Neuroscience graduate programs are welcome and should reach out to discuss setting up a rotation. Prospective undergraduates should email a description of their research interests and goals along with an unofficial transcript.
